e: From yeah or yes and hello.
q: He answered with his usual detached inflection, “Yallo.”
2012, Ann J. Colby, Cross Town Murders, page 378:
“Yallo,” his boss drawled and Seth could picture the man kicked back in his recliner, beer in hand, watching a repeat of some golden oldie sitcom on TV.
2011, Mari Carr, Jayne Rylon, Southern Comfort, page 52:

A country-boy Texas drawl, similar to Quelldon's own, spilled back from wherever the call terminated. “Yallo.” There was a small cough, then the voice repeated the mispronounced greeting. “Yallo? Anybody there?”
2004, John Powell III, Hunter And Hunted, page 440:
But I think you could safely assume that Alcott was meaner than a yalla dog about the whole thing.
1993, D. J. H. Jones, Murder at the MLA, page 200:

e: Possibly derived from Hebrew יָעֵל (ya'el, “mountain goat”). Compare Latin eale.
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish یالی (yalı), from Greek γιαλός (gialós).
From Arabic يَاللَّه (yā-llāh, “come on, hurry up”) + -ball (“suffix used to denote a specific tactical style”). Derived from the common Arabic exclamation used to encourage urgency or speed.

And it's lucky for the rest that they can't git it. I see three spears o ' yaller corn once tryin' to occoopy an acre lot. But they could n't seem to make no good use on't, an' growed yallerer an' yallerer, an' spindlin'er an' spindlin'er, till they didn't know themselves from pigeon grass.
